title: System-Design Optimization of a Single-Transmitter, Single-Fiber QKD-based ITS Communication Link
authors: Shivang Srivastava, Guillaume Ricard, Yves Jaouën, Matteo Schiavon, Romain Alléaume
abstract: Deploying QKD-based secure communication at scale requires reducing duplicated optical hardware while preserving the rate of protected user data. Earlier studies established the physical feasibility of carrying CV-QKD and classical signals over shared infrastructure, motivating a quantitative comparison between optical hardware savings and the OTP-encrypted rate. We perform this comparison by defining the secure communication rate (SCR) as the rate jointly supported by secret-key generation and classical transport, and using it to optimize a shared discrete-modulation CV-QKD link. The model combines a binomial 64-QAM security bound with a trusted receiver, protocol traffic, spectral leakage - optical power leaking into the quantum receive band - and Raman scattering. At 25 km, the asymptotic model gives an optimized SCR of 12.079 Mbps, compared with 12.095 Mbps for a separated-link reference, while reducing the transmitter and fiber counts from two to one each in the modeled direction. Increasing channel separation suppresses spectral leakage, but the resulting SCR gain diminishes once receiver bandwidth limits the rate. Under the adopted receiver-noise law, increasing the bandwidth budget from 350 to 750 MHz raises the projected 25-km SCR to 24.535 Mbps despite higher trusted electronic noise. For the studied metropolitan link, sharing saves optical resources with little rate loss, while receiver-bandwidth improvements provide greater benefit than further spectral separation. Together, these results suggest an integration path: share the transmitter and fiber, limit unwanted classical power in the quantum receive band, and increase usable receiver bandwidth where the noise budget permits.
summary: This paper optimizes the design of a QKD-based communication link for ITS by modeling the joint support of secret key generation and classical data transmission over shared optical infrastructure. The key finding is that sharing physical components saves resources with minimal rate penalty, and improving receiver bandwidth offers the most significant rate enhancement. This suggests a practical integration path for future quantum networks.
main_problem: The paper aims to optimize the system design for a shared single-transmitter, single-fiber Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) link used for Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) communication.
main_result: Sharing the transmitter and fiber resources significantly reduces hardware requirements with only a minor loss in the Secure Communication Rate (SCR) at metropolitan distances, while increasing receiver bandwidth provides a greater rate benefit than further spectral separation.
method: The authors developed a model that jointly optimizes the SCR by considering the interplay between secret-key generation, classical data transport, spectral leakage, and noise sources like Raman scattering.
model_or_system: The system models a coupled classical/CV-QKD architecture over a shared optical fiber, optimizing the rate based on a binomial 64-QAM security bound and incorporating hardware resource constraints.
key_observables: Secure Communication Rate (SCR) in Mbps, Hardware-Normalized Rate (kbit/s), and resource counts ($N_{Tx}, N_{fib}, N_{Rx/DSP}$).
important_parameters: Link distance (e.g., 25 km, 100 km), receiver bandwidth (e.g., 350 MHz to 750 MHz), and channel separation ($\Delta f$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes a trusted receiver, incorporates spectral leakage and Raman scattering, and relies on a specific receiver-noise law for optimization.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate hardware resource comparisons (separated vs. shared links) and the dependence of the SCR on various parameters like bandwidth and separation.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of resource optimization for shared QKD links, details the coupled mathematical model incorporating security and classical constraints, presents numerical results comparing shared vs. separated links, and concludes with an integrated design path.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical engineering challenges of deploying quantum networks by quantifying the trade-offs between hardware sharing, spectral management, and receiver electronics limitations.
